'''''Amaranthus caudatus''''' (also known as ''Amaranthus edulis''<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=[[US National Research Council]] |url=https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_iT0rAAAAYAAJ/page/n29/mode/2up |title=Lost Crops of the Incas: Little-Known Plants of the Andes with Promise for Worldwide Cultivation |date=1989 |publisher=National Academy Press |isbn=978-0-309-04264-2 |location=Washington, DC |pages=18, 124–127}}</ref> and ''Amaranthus mantegazzianus'')<ref name=":0" /> is an [[Andean]] species of annual [[flowering plant]]. It goes by [[common name]]s such as '''love-lies-bleeding''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | accessdate=31 July 2014}}</ref> '''pendant amaranth''',<ref>{{Cite book |last=Akeroyd |first=Simon |url=https://archive.org/details/rhsvegetablesfor0000aker/page/36 |title=RHS Vegetables for the Gourmet Gardener: Old, new, common and curious vegetables to grow and eat |publisher=[[Mitchell Beazley]] |year=2014 |isbn=978-1-84533-886-2 |location=[[United Kingdom]] |page=36 |via=the [[Internet Archive]]}}</ref> '''tassel flower''',<ref name=GRIN/> '''velvet flower''',<ref name=GRIN/> and '''foxtail amaranth'''.<ref name=GRIN/> In South America, it is known as '''kiwicha'''.<ref name=":0" /> 

Many parts of the plant, including the leaves and seeds, are edible, and sometimes exported outside of Latin America.

== Description ==

''A. caudatus'' is an [[Annual plant|annual]], broad-leaved [[dicotyledon]] with a central stem that grows from a taproot system. Depending on the variety, ''A. caudatus'' can reach up to {{Convert|2.5|m|ft|abbr=off|frac=2}} tall. Leaves and side branches grow outward from the central stem and may start as low as the base of the plant.<ref name=":0" />

''A. caudatus'' is most recognizable for its striking flowering [[Panicle|panicles]] that can reach up to {{Convert|90|cm|abbr=off}} long. The colour of these highly dense flowering panicles ranges from black, to red and more commonly white. The red varieties of ''A. caudatus'' are due to a high content of [[betacyanins]].<ref name=":0" />

Each panicle is self-pollinating and the fruits each contain a single small seed, no larger than {{Convert|1|mm|frac=32}} in diameter. Like [[quinoa]], each seed has a shiny coat and the embryo is curved around the small endosperm. The panicles grow from lateral buds and from the main stem.<ref name=":0" />

== Taxonomy ==
''A. caudatus'' is believed to be a wild ''[[Amaranthus hybridus|A. hybridus]]'' aggregate.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}}

== Etymology ==
During the [[Victorian era]], specific flowers had different meanings. Love-lies-bleeding stood for untenable romantic relationships or absence of desirable prospects in the Victorian [[language of flowers]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://davesgarden.com/guides/articles/view/3138/#b|title=Love Lies Bleeding: A Memorable Name for a Striking Plant|website=davesgarden.com|access-date=2016-11-26}}</ref> Therefore, as the plant visually resembles droplets of blood and [[Puritan]] [[virtue name]]s had been around since the 16th century, the name love-lies-bleeding is not unexpected.

== Distribution and habitat ==
''A. caudatus'' is an indigenous crop from the high Peruvian [[Andes]] that has been cultivated for thousands of years by many cultures including the [[Incas]].<ref name=":0" /> It is the only [[amaranth]] species that can grow at altitudes greater than {{Convert|2,500|m|abbr=on}} above sea level.<ref name="INIFAP">{{cite journal |last1=Espitia Rangel |first1=E. |last2=Mapes Sánchez |first2=C. |last3=Escobedo López |first3=D. |last4=De la O Olán |first4=M. |last5=Rivas Valencia |first5=P. |last6=Martínez Trejo |first6=G. |last7=Cortés Espinoza |first7=L. |last8=Hernández Casillas |first8=J.M. |title=Conservación y uso de los recursos genéticos de Amaranto en México |journal=Centro de Investigación Regional Centro |date=2010 |page=200 |publisher=INIFAP |location=Celaya, Guanjuato, México}}</ref>

== Cultivation ==
Despite the fact that ''A. caudatus'' had been a well-adapted staple in the Andean region for millennia and had offered substantial nutritional advantages to the native people, when the Spanish came in the 1500s, they replaced ''A. caudatus'' cultivations with wheat and barley. However, because of its great nutritional content, ''A. caudatus'' is regaining popularity and returning to compete with modern crops. Although ''A. caudatus'' is seldom recognized outside of the Andes, significant plantings have been observed in Mexico, China, Nepal, India and Kenya.<ref name="INIFAP" />

In most parts of its habitat, ''A. caudatus'' can easily grow between {{Convert|1 and 2.5|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} and grows best in full sun within 4–6 months. However, in some highland regions it can take up to 10 months. It is a summer annual [[C4 plant]]. It grows from [[Ecuador]] to northern [[Argentina]] mostly in mild areas or in the valleys of the Andes. Despite its geographical adaptability, it is a short-day plant and needs adequate moisture. Cultivation can occur at up to {{Convert|3100|m|abbr=on}} and once established it is [[drought tolerant]] and can handle both wet and dry conditions. If the cultivation takes place in subtropical climates, it can be harvested up to two times. [[Loam]] and loam-sandy soils with lots of organic matter and good drainage are best. [[Clay]] soils are not recommended for ''A. caudatus''. In addition, the [[Soil pH|pH]] must be between 6–7, although the plant can still grow at a pH of up to 8.5.<ref name="Fabio and Parraga">A. Di Fabio and G. Parraga, "Origin, Production and Utilization of Pseudocereals," Pseudocereals Chem. Technol., pp. 1–27, 2016, doi: 10.1002/9781118938256.ch1.</ref><ref>S. Montserrat-de la Paz, A. Martinez-lopez, A. Villanueva-lazo, J. Pedroche, F. Millan, and M. C. Millan-linares, "Identification and characterization of novel antioxidant protein hydrolysates from kiwicha (Amaranthus caudatus l.)," Antioxidants, vol. 10, no. 5, 2021, doi: 10.3390/antiox10050645.</ref>

The crop is planted by transfer, with the help of seedlings in fields or by direct drilling at the beginning of the rainy season. They are cut at a height of {{Convert|10 to 55|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} and the cultivation practices are similar to those of corn: ear emergence, two-stage fertilization and weed control. In the Andes of [[Peru]], [[Bolivia]], Ecuador and Argentina, the plant is grown in the traditional way on non-irrigated land without fertilizers. The seeds are very small, so soil preparation is important, such as breaking up of clods and shaking up. It is recommended to plough the soil, harrow and make furrows either in the traditional way with a yoke or by machine.<ref name="Fabio and Parraga" />

Weed control takes place manually with pricking out. In the absence of rain, irrigation is necessary every 30 days and especially in flowering and grain filling stages. Harvesting is done before full maturity of the plant. In this process, the plants are cut 50 cm above the ground. They are collected in furrows until they dry and then hit with sticks. In this process, they are placed on clothing or tamped floors for threshing and sieved so that the seeds can be separated from the dead leaves. Improvement of cultivation consists in proper soil preparation and direct sowing of selected seeds at a density of 4 to 6 kg/ha in 80 cm wide furrows, using fertilizers according to the nutrient content of the soil. The yield varies between 2,000 and 5,000 kg/ha in Peru and 900 to 4,000 kg/ha in Ecuador.<ref name="Fabio and Parraga" />

In indigenous agriculture, ''A. cruentus'' is the Central American counterpart to South American ''A. caudatus''.{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}}

=== Genetics === 
All species of amaranth have a [[diploid]] chromosome set but a different number of chromosomes. In ''A. caudatus'' the number is 2n = 32.<ref name="Fabio and Parraga"/>

=== Pests and diseases ===
The most common diseases affecting the seeds are [[Pythium]] spp. and [[Fusarium]] spp. Fungal diseases such as [[Sclerotinia]] spp. and [[Alternaria]] spp. cause stem and root rot. The most common pest is Diabrotica spp, also known as Loritos, which can damage the plant during emergence. Other pests include [[Agrotis]] spp. and [[Eupicata]] spp. [[Blister beetle]]s (Epicauta adspersa) and [[red weed caterpillar]] (Loxostege bifidalis) were also found in some countries. They caused severe defoliation of the upper leaves. These pests are controlled by the application of 1.5% [[diatomaceous earth]].<ref name="Fabio and Parraga"/>

== Food ==
[[File:Amaranthus_kiwicha.jpg|thumb|''Amaranthus caudatus'' grain]]

=== Nutrition ===
The flavourful and [[Gluten-free diet|gluten-free]] ''A. caudatus'' is very high in protein and essential amino acids, such as [[lysine]], which are typically deficient in plant protein. In terms of nutritional content, ''A. caudatus'' protein is virtually similar to milk protein ([[casein]]), and it complements the nutritional quality of foods derived from flours of corn, rice, or wheat.<ref name="INIFAP"/> As a result, ''A. caudatus'' is particularly beneficial for infants, children, and pregnant and lactating women, but also vegetarians and vegans.

''A. caudatus'' is high in dietary fiber and minerals such as iron, magnesium and manganese. Its frequent consumption could help to reduce hypertension and cholesterol. ''A. caudatus'' has also been found to have anthelmintic, antinociceptive, antipyretic, anticancer, antiallergenic, antidiabetic, immune system stimulation, cardioprotective, hepatoprotective, and antibacterial properties.<ref name="functionalfood">{{cite journal |vauthors=Martinez-Lopez A, Millan-Linares MC, Rodriguez-Martin NM, Millan F, Montserrat-de la Paz S |title=Nutraceutical value of kiwicha (''Amaranthus caudatus'' L.) |journal=Journal of Functional Foods |date=2020 |volume=65 |article-number=103735 |doi=10.1016/j.jff.2019.103735 |s2cid=214389327 |doi-access=free |hdl=10261/202021 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

=== Culinary use and dishes ===
{{See also|Peruvian cuisine}}
There are several uses of kiwicha. When ground, it can be used as flour but also as breading for sweets and main dishes when crushed. Seeds can be popped like popcorn in a pan and, like oats, it can be eaten with milk as cereal.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="lima">{{cite web |author=Sunflower|date=May 7, 2021 |title=Kiwicha |website=Lima easy |url=https://www.limaeasy.com/peruvian-food-guide/grain-coffee-crop-beans-and-nuts/kiwicha#:~:text=The%20grain%20is%20also%20ground,of%20Peru's%20%22super%20grains%22.}}</ref><ref name="Marx">{{cite journal |last1=Marx |first1=J. L. |title=Amaranth: A Comeback for the Food of the Aztecs? |journal=Science |date=1977 |volume=198|issue=4312 |page=40 |doi=10.1126/science.198.4312.40 |pmid=17741884 |s2cid=33605799 }}</ref>

In Mexico, ''A. caudatus'' is used on sweets with honey; the dish is called {{Lang|es|alegria}} ({{Gloss|happiness}} in Spanish). India has a similar dish called ''ladoos''.<ref name=":0" /> ''A. caudatus'' is slowly making its way outside of Latin America. Cookies and other breakfast food made of kiwicha can be found, for example, in stores in the United States.<ref name=":0" /> Even though kiwicha is gluten-free, adding kiwicha flour to wheat when producing leavened food increases the nutritional value of the bread.<ref name=":0" /> As flour, ''A. caudatus'' is also used for pasta and noodles.<ref name="functionalfood"/>

Due to the food's nutritional value, scientists have explored the substitution of amaranth leaves for certain vegetables in traditional Kenyan traditional dishes. They have also investigated whether the vitamins and minerals remain when boiled, for instance. Depending on the vegetables used in the mix, mineral and iron uptake can be improved.<ref name="Nyonje">{{cite journal |vauthors=Nyonje WA, Yang RY, Wu WJ, Makokha AO, Owino WO, Abukutsa-Onyango MO |title=Enhancing the Nutritional Quality of Vegetable Amaranth through Specific Food Preparation Methods |journal=Journal of Food Research |date=2021 |volume=10 |issue=4 |pages=42–55|doi=10.5539/jfr.v10n4p42 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Other uses ==

=== Animal feed ===
After the ''A. caudatus'' grains have been removed, the remaining plant material ([[stover]]) can be used for [[fodder]]. During dry seasons when [[forage]] is limited, fodder from ''A. caudatus'' stover is an essential source of animal feed for Andean farmers to maintain their livestock.<ref name=":0" />

Additionally, ''A. caudatus'' can be suitable to be used as a high-protein forage crop in the [[tropics]].<ref name=":0" />

=== Natural dye ===
In Peru, simple methods have been developed to extract [[betalain]] from red varieties of ''A. caudatus'' to be used as non-toxic red food colouring. For some applications, this natural dye may be used to replace the use of synthetic dyes. However natural dyes tend to have a lower [[colour fastness]] and therefore may not function well as a direct substitution.<ref name=":0" />

==Regional names==
To the [[Quechua people]] of South America, ''A. caudatus'' is referred to as kiwicha, quihuicha, inca jataco; ataco, ataku, sankurachi, jaguarcha (Ecuador), millmi, or coimi.<ref name=":0" /> While to the [[Aymara people]], who are native to the Andes and [[Altiplano]] regions of South America, ''A. caudatus'' is known as qamasa.<ref name=":0" />
